World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Jay Vine escapes serious injury after horrifying crash at Giro d'Italia
World.content:
Australian cyclist Jay Vine has escaped serious injury in his horrifying crash on stage two of the Giro d'Italia in Bulgaria on Saturday.

The 30-year-old was confirmed by UAE Team Emirates-XRG to have suffered a fractured elbow and concussion — neither of which will require surgery.

However, the accident could have been much worse.

Vine was taken out when UAE Team Emirates-XRG teammate Mark Soler's front wheel lost traction on a slippery descent with 22km remaining on the second stage of this year's race.

Several riders came down, with UAE Team Emirates-XRG particularly badly affected as Soler, Vine and team leader Adam Yates all smashed into the armco barrier at high speed.

Vine appeared to be riding immediately behind Soler and had nowhere to go, sliding and hitting the metal barrier with sickening force.

Yates, too, was particularly badly affected, landing sideways on top of the barrier and ending up covered in a mix of blood and mud before riding on to the finish, losing 14 minutes to the race leaders.

"Unfortunately, we were badly affected by the crash on stage two yesterday," Dr Adrian Rotunno, UAE Team Emirates' medical director, said on Sunday.

"Jay Vine suffered a concussion and an elbow fracture. Marc Soler has a pelvic fracture. At this stage, neither should require surgery.

"Adam Yates suffered heavy abrasions and a laceration to his left ear. He was initially assessed on-site for concussion and cleared to continue, but subsequently, he has shown delayed concussive symptoms. He will not take the start of stage three today.

"All three are under observation of our medical staff and will travel home in the coming days to continue their recovery and rehab."

Vine was initially complaining about pain in the same arm that he broke at the Tour Down Under in January, according to UAE directeur sportif Fabio Baldato, as he was taken to the hospital.

Jay Vine was stretchered to hospital. (Supplied: SBS)

Vine, the Australian time trial champion and world silver medallist against the clock, had been hoping to challenge for victory on stage 10's 42km race of truth.

The incident once again brought into stark relief the risk of modern cycling, where high speeds and high stakes combine in a terrifying mix.

Fifteen years to the day on from the death of Belgian sprinter Wouter Weylandt, who died of injuries caused by a heavy crash on the descent from the Passo del Bocco on the 2011 edition of the Giro d'Italia, cycling did not need another reminder of the fragility of its key protagonists.

The intrinsic failings and risks of cycling laid bare with another premature death Cycling has lost another rider due to a downhill crash, with teenager Muriel Furrer killed on a descent at the World Championships in Zurich. So where does the responsibility lie?

Colombian rider Cristian Camilo Munoz died from a knee infection six days after crashing at the Tour du Jura in France in April, just the latest in an increasingly long list of fatalities within the professional peloton.

Earlier this season, British rider Tom Pidcock was fortunate to avoid the worst when he fell down a ravine on the fifth stage of the Volta Ciclista a Catalunya.

"It was like one of these horror crashes you see … I am lucky I could talk on the radio," Pidcock said at the time.

"I was far from the road and nobody knew I was there. Sixty kilometres per hour off a mountain road and I'm relatively OK."

In 2024, Swiss teenager Muriel Furrer was not so lucky, lying undiscovered for 82 minutes after crashing during a junior women's road race at the world championships in Zurich, and dying at the scene.

Norway's André Drege died at the Tour of Austria that same year, with Swiss rider Gino Mäder dying after crashing into a ravine on the descent of the Albula Pass at the Tour de Suisse in 2023.

This Bulgarian pile-up was 30-year-old Vine's third serious crash in 13 race days this year.

Jay Vine withdrew from the Volta a Catalunya after a crash on stage three. (Getty Images: Szymon Gruchalski)

He was taken out by a kangaroo at the Tour Down Under in January — a race he ended up winning despite riding for over 70 with what his team described as "a significant left wrist scaphoid fracture" that required surgery — and the Volta Ciclista a Catalunya in March.

Incredibly, that Catalunya crash was Vine's 22nd crash in the last five years, according to ProCyclingStats data.

None was more serious than his 2022 terrifying tumble at the Itzulia Basque Country that left him with a fractured skull and vertebrae, leaving him with fears he may never walk again.

Then, as is the case now, Vine's wife, Bre, normally a notable presence roadside during Vine's races, was watching on from home while pregnant — no doubt reliving those awful days from 2022 in harrowing detail.

Bre Vine (left) is normally roadside for husband Jay Vine's races, but his crashes are never easy to witness. (Getty Images: James Raison)

Plenty of riders were critical of the Giro in the aftermath of the crash, with Jasper Stuyven (Soudal Quick-Step) particularly caustic with his opinion of race director Stefano Allocchio, who restarted the race just minutes after it was neutralised as a result of the crash.

"There were no ambulances left on course, but there was still a descent ahead that could have been dangerous," Stuyven told Belgian media HLN.

"After a crash like that, we wanted a neutralisation of the GC times, the brave ones could still race for the stage win — but on that next descent, there was no need for anyone to take unnecessary risks.

"The race director said they were looking at it. Then, like a scared dog, he stuck his head out of the car, started waving his flag and shouted 'race' — before quickly pulling his head back inside."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

However, it is hard to see what the race organisers could do to make races 100 per cent safe aside from neutralising the race every time it rains.

"I think everyone could see that someone was going to fall on these roads, and we were the unlucky ones," UAE's Portuguese rider António Morgado told Eurosport.

"Everyone knew the roads would be very slippery, and that's exactly why everyone wanted to be at the front."

Nevertheless, the incident showed once again that cycling is a risky pursuit.

World.title: Phoenix makes A-League history with semifinal triumph over Brisbane
World.content:
Wellington Phoenix is just one win away from its first A-League Women's crown after defeating Brisbane Roar 2-0 after extra time to advance to the grand final.

Makala Woods grabbed a first-half goal and added a second in the first period of extra time at Porirua Park on Sunday to help Wellington overcome a first-leg deficit and down the Roar 3-2 on aggregate.

The Phoenix, who finished the regular season in second spot, will meet premiers Melbourne City at AAMI Park next Saturday, when they will become the first side from New Zealand to feature in an A-League grand final.

Wellington entered the ALW in 2021 and became perennial strugglers, missing the finals in the past four seasons.

But the arrival of former Canada coach Bev Priestman in the off-season has turned the Phoenix into contenders.

Priestman coached Canada at the Paris Olympics and received a year-long ban for using drones to spy on opponents.

City surges into ALW grand final after young gun's stunning strike Shelby McMahon fires Melbourne City into the A-League Women's grand final, with her side downing Melbourne Victory 2-0 on aggregate.

"It's amazing, we've been working for this for five years," said Wellington captain Mackenzie Barry.

"We've had such a hard season, the girls have been amazing, Bev's been amazing, and I'm so happy and can't wait for next week.

"It's overwhelming and I feel so proud of this club, we've gone through it — had two bottom of the table (finishes) — and now we've been building up, and we're in the final."

Brisbane led 2-1 coming into Sunday's second leg, but found their advantage erased in the 42nd minute when Woods found the back of the net.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

The 'Nix played long on the counter and American striker Woods beat the offside trap to dart in on goal and poke her shot beyond the reach of Chloe Lincoln to level the tie.

Woods was twice denied by Lincoln as the Phoenix pushed for a late winner to send the game into extra time.

But after Matildas star Tameka Yallop was forced off with a hamstring injury, Woods hit home in the 102nd minute when Angie Beard misjudged a Brooke Nunn cross.

Woods was able to benefit from Beard's error and the 23-year-old striker, who has seven goals in 14 games since arriving in the ALW in January, finished past Lincoln to send Wellington into their first grand final.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Netball body suspends woman charged over alleged antisemitic slur at game
World.content:
A woman has been charged after allegedly making antisemitic comments during an under-12 girls netball game in Sydney.

Officers attended Heffron Park in Maroubra about 10am on Saturday, following reports of offensive comments made during a match between Maccabi Netball Club and Saints Netball Club.

A 42-year-old woman was spoken to at the scene and issued with a move-on order, but was not arrested.

On Sunday, she was charged and issued with a Court Attendance Notice for using offensive language in or near a public place or school.

She was due to appear at Waverley Local Court on Wednesday, June 17.

Mr Ryvchin confronted the woman, 42, over the alleged incident. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin, who attended the scene after the incident, said the woman allegedly told parents and players associated with the opposing club, "F*** the Jews", adding that Jewish people "should have been eradicated".

"A man walked past and heard her and asked her what she said and she repeated the phrase," Mr Ryvchin claimed.

In a video supplied to the ABC, Mr Ryvchin could be seen confronting the woman over the alleged incident.

"Did you actually say what's being alleged," Mr Ryvchin said in the video.

"No," the woman said multiple times.

"Oh my god, so are we going to call the police," she added, before saying she was happy to speak to them.

The alleged incident took place on Saturday morning at Heffron Park, in Maroubra. (ABC News: Thorsten Joses )

'No immediate consequences'

Mr Ryvchin said other parents associated with the Saints club came forward to defend the woman after she was confronted.

"One man was recorded saying that 'There's a reason why this happens to you people every weekend', and 'You're always playing the victim'," he said.

"We're all families, Australian families, just watching our kids play and having a good time and enjoying the weekend. It's disgusting."

Impact of antisemitism on kids heard at inquiry Unlike her idyllic childhood, Natalie Levy's children now attend school surrounded by security and swastikas graffitied on buildings.

He said he was disappointed the Saints Netball Club had not acted swiftly to condemn the woman's alleged behaviour during the match.

"The first response should have been from the woman's own club, from other parents on her team to say, 'You have brought us into disgrace'," he said.

"This is just not acceptable in any circumstance. They should have moved her on.

"There are no immediate consequences. People don't know how to react and therefore it becomes tolerated."

'Provisionally suspended'

In a statement posted online, the Saints Netball Club said it "unequivocally condemns and disavows antisemitism in all forms".

"Such remarks do not reflect the values, principles, or standards of our club, our members, our players, or our wide community," the statement said.

" The Saints Netball Club offers our sincerest and most unreserved apologies to the Jewish community and to those affected. "

Randwick Netball Association said it would not tolerate antisemitic or discriminatory behaviour.

"We are working with Netball NSW to apply the applicable integrity framework as we investigate and respond to the matter," the statement said.

Mark Falvo, Netball Australia's interim CEO, said the local and state bodies had their "full support", and that there were repercussions for the woman involved.

"The individual alleged to have made the comments has been provisionally suspended from attending or participating in any netball activities or attending netball locations while the matter is investigated," he said in a statement.

"We will continue to engage with the local netball and Jewish communities and work together to send a message that netball is safe and inclusive for all."

The ABC has made attempts to contact the woman involved.

NSW Energy Minister Penny Sharpe called the alleged incident "absolutely unacceptable". (ABC News)

On Sunday, NSW Energy Minister Penny Sharpe said she was "horrified" by the "absolutely unacceptable" alleged incident.

"Kids playing sport on a Saturday morning, particularly Jewish kids, should not have to deal with that — nor should their families," she said.

Comments come amid Royal Commission

The incident comes after the first week of hearings at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

AJAX football club president Daniel Onas told the inquiry this week there had been an "unprecedented" rise in incidents in community sport, including players being told "Hitler should have finished you off", and a Jewish parent being called "a bloody Jew" during a match.

Mr Ryvchin said he hoped the woman involved in the netball incident would receive a life ban from attending future games, saying it was "a perfect case study of what has been going on in our society for too long".

World.title: Fuel injection as SA announces $40m diesel stockpile
World.content:
Emergency diesel supplies will be sourced from Singapore to create a strategic reserve in South Australia, with the state government today announcing $40 million in spending to bolster fuel stocks amid uncertainty arising from the Iran war.

It said the plan to purchase 10 to 20 million litres would inject what amounted to, in terms of current consumption, an extra four days' worth of diesel into the state's current stockpile.

The government, which previously rejected state-based approaches to the issue, today said the extra diesel would be stored at bulk fuel supplier IOR's facility at Port Bonython near Whyalla in the Upper Spencer Gulf, and that the move was largely intended to provide certainty to the state's farmers.

"This is a reserve — it's going to be here in case there's an emergency. And it doesn't fix every problem if there [is], but it just gives us a degree of confidence into the future," Premier Peter Malinauskas said.

"We are acquiring this reserve for the worst of circumstances, if it presents itself.

"This is not an everyday transaction. This is a very unique event."

Under the plan, fuel will be stored at Port Bonython. (Federal Government)

Grain Producers SA welcomed the reserve, saying it would provide extra assurance to primary producers.

"With the uncertainty of the ongoing war, what's going to happen with fuel and fertiliser supply in the long term is relatively unknown, so South Australia needs to be doing everything we can to keep farmers farming," CEO Brad Perry said in a statement.

Corbin Schuster, who produces grain and hay at Freeling, about 65 kilometres north of Adelaide, and was currently seeding crops, said the magnitude of recent spikes in the price of fuel had come as a shock to the sector.

"When things kicked off over there in the Gulf, it was a concern for us," Mr Schuster said.

" On our farm we'd be using probably over 200,000 litres a year. "

Freeling farmer Corbin Schuster says he typically buys fuel in bulk. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

He said while many farmers had their own on-site fuel storage, extra supply was a "good outcome".

"This strategic fuel reserve for South Australia — hopefully we never have to use it — but if we can set it up, it's there for the long term," he said.

Last week, the federal government announced the upcoming budget would include a $10 billion funding package aimed at increasing Australia's fuel stockpiles.

Move overdue, opposition says

The new reserve would include an initial purchase of 10 million litres as well as an option to double that amount, the government said.

Mr Malinauskas described it as a contingency plan, and said it was not an indicator of imminent supply restrictions.

"It's approximately four days' worth of diesel supply on top of around about 30 days that is currently here," he said.

"If you're quarantining it for very specific purposes, it's a lot more than that."

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas today signed an agreement with IOR CEO Drew Morland. (ABC News)

In mid-April the WA government announced it was creating its own "strategic stockpile" amounting to 4 million litres of diesel, but SA Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis rejected that approach.

"What we need is the Australian government coordinating this nationally. We don't want states competing with the Australian government to purchase fuel," he told 891 ABC Adelaide on April 15.

"States going out and arbitrarily buying fuel is probably not in the national interest."

The SA opposition, which had previously called for the creation of a strategic reserve, said an extra 20 million litres of diesel would hit "the sweet spot".

"That'll mean that our agricultural industry can run for two weeks if there is a complete [cut to] the supply chain," Liberal leader Ashton Hurn said.

" It's exactly what a smart government should be doing because we know that farmers in particular — but our state more broadly — can't run off the smell of an oily rag. "

Liberal leader Ashton Hurn says the plan should have been adopted weeks ago. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

She said the decision to create a reserve signalled a "change of tune" from the government.

"We think that when we called it for it three weeks ago, the government could have recognised a good idea, but it's really only been over the last couple of days that they've started to reinvent history a little bit," she said.

"Why didn't they come out when we proposed it in the middle of April and say this is a fantastic idea?"

Mr Malinauskas, who today signed an agreement with fuel supplier IOR, said the government had "been negotiating" with the company since March.

IOR CEO Drew Morland said the company was committed to working with governments "to unlock the ability to store more fuel in country to keep industry moving".

World.title: When Nicole started checking her breasts, she never expected to find a lump
World.content:
When Nicole Speirs made the conscious decision to start checking her breasts regularly, she never expected she would find any changes.

But a few months in, her self-examination found a lump.

"It was very, very unexpected," she said.

"I'm very, very fortunate my past self … started doing that."

The 32-year-old had no family history nor risk factors for breast cancer.

Nicole Speirs was diagnosed with breast cancer 18 months ago. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

But an ultrasound and biopsy found cancer in her lymph nodes in December 2024.

"It was a massive, massive upheaval of everything for not only me, but my network, my family, my partner, my workplace," she recalled.

"My mum took a sabbatical at the time. She was here every other week, coming to treatment with me.

"And then my partner as well — we'd only met two months prior to my diagnosis, so we had some very hard and very tough conversations, and he's been amazing and supported me through the journey."

Ms Speirs said they "threw every treatment possible at it" and she was "now cancer-free".

"But it is something that I still live with every day," she said.

"It's something that the side effects of the chemo, radiation, surgery, I'm still managing, and I'm also on preventative medicine to move forward."

As part of her recovery, Nicole Speirs has taken up dragon boating with Dragons Abreast. The group took to Canberra's Lake Burley Griffin for today's Mother's Day Classic. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Her experience, she said, "brought everything into perspective".

"It's meant that my relationships are much richer and much stronger," Ms Speirs said.

"It's such a horrible thing for all of us to go through [but] it's really brought us all together."

Mother's Day Classic fundraisers

When Ms Speirs tried to make an appointment for her first ultrasound before her diagnosis, she recalls being told there was a months-long wait.

But "fortunately", she was impatient, and kept calling different providers until she was able to secure an earlier appointment.

"That's an experience that a lot of other women I've spoken to have had, that they can't get in quickly for scans," she said.

"So that's something that's really important to raise funds, raise awareness, because with breast cancer, the earlier detection, the better your outcome is going to be."

This year's event started from Lennox Gardens, and included 5km and 10km courses. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Ms Speirs joined some 4,500 people along the shore of Canberra's Lake Burley Griffin this morning for the Mother's Day Classic charity fun run and walk.

Today marks the 20th year that the event has been held in Canberra, and was one of more than 90 fundraisers held across the country to raise funds and awareness for breast and ovarian cancers.

"Canberra always punches above its weight because we have a wonderful, wonderful community here," Canberra Mother's Day Classic chairwoman Leeanne Turner said.

"[From] very humble beginnings 20 years ago, we've just seen numbers build and build and build as the event's gotten bigger and bigger and bigger.

" It's important for so many people who have lost their lives or are battling with breast cancer or ovarian cancer. "

Leeanne Turner says Canberra "punches above its weight" when it comes to fundraising for the Mother's Day Classic. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

The Mother's Day Classic began in Sydney and Melbourne in 1998, and has since raised more than $50 million nationally, funding 100 research projects.

During that time, the five-year relative survival rate for breast cancer has "improved dramatically", Ms Turner said, and now sits around 93 per cent.

I lost a breast to cancer, but I still enjoy the one I have I decided to keep my healthy breast, opting against reconstruction. It means I'm now what's known in the community as a uniboober.

Ms Turner said they want to see "the same lift" in the ovarian cancer five-year relative survival rate, which is currently only 49 per cent.

"The problem with ovarian cancer, and why those statistics are so low, is that it's hard to find. Once it is found, it's in the late stages, so that makes it very difficult," she said.

"It would be great if we can find a quicker, better detection, particularly for ovarian cancer.

"And what we're able to do through this magnificent event is to raise those vital funds that are needed for breast and ovarian cancer research."

It is the 20th year the Mother's Day Classic has been held in Canberra. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

As the research continues, Ms Speirs urged women to make sure they do regular breast checks.

"I know that's a thing that we hear and we don't do," she said.

"Pick a time in the month, do it every month, and you'll notice the changes and then you can do something about it.

"Even if you don't have risk factors, it can happen."

Sabalenka needed treatment late in ​her meeting with ‌Cirstea on Saturday before she fell 2-6, 6-3, 7-5 for her second defeat in three matches after a quarterfinal loss to Hailey Baptiste ‌at the Madrid Open last month.
